There is a risk that today’s popular government could become the maker of tomorrow’s climate disaster.

Nepal is not separate from this broad global trend. In Nepal, this question cannot be read merely as a theoretical one. Here, a newly elected government has come with extraordinary popularity, an aspiration for quick decisions, and a mandate of deep distrust towards the old political parties. The rise of Balendra Shah is a product of this very restlessness. But every popular elected leader faces this question: Can they transform the popularity into democratic tolerance? Because the early signals of Shah’s rule also remind us that popularity is not proof of democracy.

Democracy expects even more from the leader whom the people strongly support. If he fears the press, his popularity becomes his weakness. If he treats criticism as hostility, his mandate slowly turns into arrogance. If he sees the climate crisis as an obstacle to development, he punishes the generations of the future for the applause of the present.

We have to see whether, even when an elected government has a majority, it still listens to the voice of the minority. Whether, when the press writes against it, it improves its decisions instead of breaking the spine of the press. Whether, instead of destroying nature in the name of development, it also includes the rights of future citizens in its decisions.

Returning to that question itching the tea shop dwellers in Madhesh. “Where is our MP?” The one we elected—is the MP still among us? And if not, is the MP at least listening to our voice? The future of democracy may depend less on how fast power moves and more on how much it listens.

articles.title: Is manufacturing really expensive in Nepal?
articles.summary:
Nepal’s trade statistics for the last fiscal year have recently been released. They show that the country imported goods worth Rs2.1 trillion in 2025-26 and exported Rs315 billion. For every rupee we sold to the world, we bought Rs6.65 from it. We recorded a trade deficit with 134 of the 162 countries we traded with, notably with most countries poorer than us. The usual explanation for this is that manufacturing is expensive in Nepal. But is that the only reason? Or are there other factors that make us a consumption nation?

Let’s see the worsening trade direction. Imports grew by 16.2 percent last year while exports grew by 13.8 percent. The trade deficit widened by 16.6 percent to Rs1.78 trillion, which is the largest on record. This figure is a part of a longer trend. Manufacturing has dropped to 4.37 percent of GDP, less than half of its 1996 share and below the world average. Overall, the industry has fallen from 15 percent of GDP to 12.8 percent in a decade.

Nepali economy is already losing its factory base before it has properly built one, which, in economics, is known as premature deindustrialisation. Services now account for 62 percent of GDP, which looks modern on paper but cannot absorb our youth bulge, leading to rising youth out-migration.

The export figure is flattering. Nepal’s largest export item is processed soybean oil, at Rs129 billion or roughly 41 percent of everything we sold abroad. This oil is refined from crude we import from Argentina and Brazil and ship on to India under preferential tariffs. Argentina is now our third-largest import partner, selling us Rs116 billion of crude oil in a year when we sold goods worth Rs18,000 to the country. If we exclude this arbitrage-driven trading, our true exports are closer to Rs186 billion against Rs2 trillion of imports, a ratio above 10 to one. What remains is revealing: Cardamom, carpets, jute, fruit juice and chhurpi, now worth Rs4 billion a year in American pet shops. These small numbers demonstrate that when production relies on Nepali materials and skills, it can compete in the toughest markets worldwide.

Now let’s examine imports. For each item, ask yourself, does making this require anything Nepal lacks? Aside from fuel, machinery and smartphones, we don’t expect to drill oil or fabricate chips. But last year, we imported roughly Rs11 billion of soap, Rs21 billion of cosmetics, Rs18 billion of packaged foods, Rs18 billion of paper and Rs74 billion of plastic goods. None of this is technically demanding. The agricultural imports are even harder to justify: A country that calls itself agricultural imported nearly Rs60 billion of cereals, Rs38 billion of vegetables and Rs35 billion of fruit, part of an agro basket approaching Rs380 billion. Ironically, we imported Rs44 billion of apparel while exporting only Rs13 billion.

The import data reveals something that our private sector should pay attention to. Each of those numbers represents an existing market with proven demand and counted volumes. Rs74 billion of plastics is not a niche; it represents the scale needed for a serious manufacturing plant, available to any investor willing to start one. Yet few of our large businesses manufacture goods; most import, distribute and take a margin. Policy support follows production, not the other way around. If Nepali capital begins by investing in the goods we already buy in billions, the state will have every reason to protect that investment and industries will gain the standing to demand it. Customs data shows demand and scale, but is there a willingness to produce?

Remittances have reached around Rs1.7 trillion a year, amounting to roughly a quarter of GDP. A young man leaves because there are no factory jobs, earns wages abroad and sends them home; the family spends that money on imported goods; the imports cross the border, where the government taxes them; the taxes pay the officials who discuss industrialisation. The reason capital doesn’t break this cycle is that we have made trading the logical choice. An importer can turn capital over within weeks at low risk. A manufacturer must find industrial land, which can take years, borrow at interest rates of 9 to 12 percent, train workers and wait two or three years to break even, all while competing with imported goods already on the shelves.

Our banking data confirm the trend: Trading companies command a larger share of bank credit than the combined manufacturing and processing industries. The government also has a stake in this. Just over Rs1 trillion of government revenue was collected at the border on imports last year, in the form of duties, VAT and excise, close to half of all treasury receipts. A government that funds its salaries through import volumes has a vested interest in keeping them high. When import substitution and payroll needs pull in opposite directions, payroll typically wins.

Beneath these incentives lies a straightforward problem—scale. A factory’s cost per unit decreases as it produces more. Our firms are small, which makes their goods expensive. That is what expensive really means in this context, and we have faced the consequences of overlooking this before. Our garment industry, once the top export earner at about Rs12 billion a year, had a decade’s warning that quota protection would end in 2005. Rather than merging into bigger plants, firms stayed small and re-stamped imported goods for quick margins. When the quotas went, so did the industry.

Cement shows the opposite. Two decades ago, we imported 90 percent of our cement; today we make our own, with turnover near Rs150 billion and exports to India. Everything lined up: limestone in our hills, a product too heavy to import cheaply, demand large enough for scale, foreign partners who financed large plants and state help through export subsidies and cheaper power. Cement succeeded despite policy but because policy, for once, supported what we could naturally do well.

The goal is to reduce production costs and make the process reliable—what one might call policy bullet-proofing. Make industrial land available without years of limbo. Price surplus electricity for industry at predictable tariffs, not just as an export. Clear VAT refunds so working capital stops dying in queues. Take agro-processing off the foreign-investment negative list, where our own law bars the capital our food bill begs for. Give the SEZ regime a workable export threshold and harmonised rules. Keep raw-material duties a tier below finished-goods duties, the one sound principle the last budget preserved and offer infant industries support that is time-bound and tied to performance. Above all, maintain stable policies long enough for a three-year investment to outlast the government that approved it. Stability is the most cost-effective support a developing country can provide.

Is manufacturing expensive in Nepal? It is expensive to manufacture poorly, in small batches, on land that took years to secure, under rules that change every year. It is not inherently expensive to manufacture well. However, our government lacks the willingness to earn revenue outside of border taxes, and our private sector is hesitant to build what it currently imports.

articles.title: Cockroach movement brought down a minister. Real reform will be much harder
articles.summary:
Over the past few weeks, young people have mobilised to protest India’s broken education system, against the background of a shortage of job opportunities.

The protests were initially sparked by the cancellation of a medical school entrance exam after questions were leaked, leading some despondent young people to take their own lives. The movement repurposed the image of a cockroach as their symbol—inspired by a comment by India’s chief justice, allegedly comparing jobless young people to “cockroaches”. Humour and satire were integral to the recent unrest.

On Saturday, the cockroach movement claimed its biggest victory since the protests began with the resignation of India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

But this move will only do so much. These issues did not appear overnight, nor can they be easily fixed.

Decades of frustration

Irregularities and shortcomings in education, as well as rampant unemployment, have been major issues in northern India since at least the early 1970s. One of the main reasons for this is the economic growth that occurred in the late 20th century was not accompanied by broad-based investment in education. It also failed to create jobs in the private sector, leaving many young people dependent on government jobs.

As I wrote in my book Timepass: Youth, Class and the Politics of Waiting in India, for example, by the late 1990s, thousands of graduates were chasing a single government job in the northern city of Meerut.

In response, many young people engaged in what they called “timepass”—spending time hanging out at street corners while continuing to study for degrees. One set of students started a club called “Generation Nowhere”.

Many of the young people I interviewed were bitter about their predicament. Many could not afford the best schools. The education system was also rife with problems, from the frequent leaks of exam papers to teacher shortages.

When I was doing fieldwork relating to young people and social change in the state of Uttar Pradesh in 2004, I met students satirically campaigning for their “democratic right to cheat” in examinations. Like the young people at the heart of the cockroach movement, these students, too, complained of questions being leaked in advance of exams and the cheating inherent in the educational system.

They also believed talented students were cheated out of a job after graduating because of the scale of unemployment in India. “Why shouldn’t we cheat, when the system is cheating us?”, one student quipped.

Students also said the system of applying for government jobs was unfair. One told me: “Everywhere, you need source [social connections] and force [money power]”.

Today’s distinctive challenges

Young people today have similar feelings of anger and being stuck in limbo. But their daily realities have changed.

As Avishek Jha and Nilanjana Sen, two researchers at the University of Melbourne, recently argued, Indian youth are often channelling considerable effort into preparing for government exams, rather than engaging in “timepass”. This reflects a growing awareness of the real threat of youth unemployment in India and a determination to find ways to maximise their chances.

An enormous number of “tuition centres” or cram schools, coaching centres, and study spaces have emerged to cater to this more driven generation, but the odds stacked against young people in competition for scant government jobs remain the same. Cockroach protesters are frustrated by all the effort and resources they are forced to expend to prepare for exams that don’t ultimately lead to better lives.

This points to the deeper, systemic problems at the heart of India’s massive youth unemployment problem.

Four main issues to address

With their main demands now met by the government, those in the cockroach movement will likely shift their focus to these broader questions of fairness in education and employment.

First, tackling structural educational problems is an obvious priority. This may require decentralising the management of examinations. But as Professor Manisha Priyam pointed out in research in Bihar, the problem is wider than the leaking of examination papers. The government must also better regulate tuition and coaching centres to ensure their marketing and activities are transparent and above board.

Second, many Indian commentators are again emphasising the issue of job creation. The government should also look at ways to improve work-integrated learning to give students better training in key fields.

Another priority is reforming school and university courses so young people can obtain the skills necessary to compete for private and public jobs, while also creating opportunities for themselves through start-ups.

This is linked to a third issue—greater investment in schooling and higher education. Sixty years ago, a commission set up by the government to examine the state of education in India recommended the government increase spending to 6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). This hasn’t happened: spending is currently just 4.1 percent.

Several experts have pointed out that education investment also needs to be smart. It should be targeted at curriculum review, improving the performances of institutions and staff, and speeding up the technological and infrastructural transformation in education.

A final theme emerging from the cockroach movement is the need for Indian authorities across the board to respect and value young people. This starts with a better understanding of the capabilities, talents and skills of those in gen Z.

Where to look for inspiration

Crucially, the cockroach movement is focusing attention on the realities of mainstream, public education—starting in primary schools—rather than simply what is happening in elite institutions.

There are some important initiatives underway that build on India’s National Education Policy. But to take a holistic approach to education reform and job creation, Indian policymakers should also look at developments in other large, developing countries, such as Brazil.

Policymakers must also look at India’s own history of successful community-government partnerships.

Above all, reforms that involve young people should now be the priority. Those in the cockroach movement have demonstrated their desire to become genuine collaborators in education reform. They deserve a seat at the table.

articles.title: SKINCARE: Navigating skin reactions triggered by UV rays
articles.summary:
The heat of summer is currently at its peak in Nepal. When the temperature soars in the season, so do the skincare worries. With oily skin, acne flare-ups and irritations, there is one more issue that adds on to the list—that is, photosensitivity. It is when your skin is exposed to UV radiation that you develop an itchy red rash. Although its severity might be heightened during the summer, people who are prone to photosensitivity should take precautions throughout the year, as UV rays are present in every season.

Dr Tapan Pradhan, co-founder and director of Kayakalpa skin and hair clinic shares the causes of photosensitivity and simple preventive tips. He is also a dermatologist at Aavaran Skin and Hair Clinic.

What is photosensitivity, and what are its most common causes?

In simple terms, photosensitivity can be understood as an abnormal immune system reaction to sunlight or UV rays. Mostly, it forms red rashes, patches, skin discolouration and blisters around your skin. There is not a specific type of reaction and it can vary from person to person. Along with sunlight, tanning beds can also trigger photosensitive reactions.

But medical conditions and certain products can also be attributed to its causes:

Lupus erythematosus

Photoeczemas,

Porphyria (a rare metabolic disorder)

Polymorphic light eruption (PMLE) — the most common form

Xeroderma pigmentosum (a genetic condition)

Certain antibiotics, diuretics, and antifungals

Chemotherapy drugs

Nutritional deficiencies (B3 vitamin)

How can people tell the difference between photosensitivity and a regular sunburn?

This is a common misconception most people have. Anyone can develop a sunburn after staying outside for too long. But a photosensitivity reaction only happens to some people. It is not that uncommon in Nepal, and I have seen such persistence in long durations with many of my clients too; however, not everyone is prone to it.

Sunburn takes time to become visible, while a photosensitive reaction can develop within minutes to a few hours after sun exposure, depending on the underlying cause, the person's skin sensitivity, and the intensity of UV exposure. It is not as serious a medical concern as photosensitivity.

When you get a sunburn, your skin is heated and it can feel painful. On the other hand, with photosensitive reactions, there might be a sharp pain, similar to ant bites. Blisters can also gradually be spotted. In more severe cases, the reaction can progress to even induce a fever.

What precautions should people take to protect their skin if they are prone to photosensitivity?

When dermatologists recommend active ingredients such as retinol or tretinoin for nighttime use, it is for good reason. Applying them during the day can make the skin more susceptible to UV damage and trigger photosensitive reactions. First precaution, is timely usage of skincare products, rather than assuming that it can be applied whenever possible.

Secondly, opting for mineral sunscreens is a good option for sun protection and should be reapplied from time to time throughout the day. Remember to choose a broad-spectrum sunscreen, as it protects against both UVA and UVB rays. A generous amount of it should be applied to all the areas prone to sun exposure.

Also, as I mentioned earlier, actively searching and testing whether the antibiotics and antifungal medicines we consume have been activating sensitive skin reactions is important.

Other precautions are simple: preventing active sunlight during the peak hours of 10-4 and carrying an umbrella at all times.

What should someone do if they experience a photosensitive reaction right after sun exposure?

After you spot a reaction, I recommend immediately covering the skin part with a damp cloth, not ice, as a sudden temperature change can further irritate the skin.

If you are aware that your skin is more photosensitive, try to include fragrance-free moisturisers in your daily routine; that is helpful. Avoid scratching or rubbing the infected area.

Over time, according to the nature of the condition, steroids might also be prescribed by dermatologists to control the symptoms.

What happens when skin photosensitivity remains untreated?

Thinking that it's a temporary problem, which can fix itself on its own, is a mistake. Actively discarding the issue and not applying any preventive measures can ultimately lead to chronic inflammation, accelerated ageing, hyperpigmentation, post-inflammatory pigmentation and even scarring.

Not only that, but avoiding the sun or going out develops into a psychological fear after some time. This is a recurring problem, and people who are photosensitive might have to stay guarded with their skincare for a long period in their lives; thus, it shouldn’t be taken very lightly. Patients may develop anxiety at the thought of stepping outside, fearing that even a few minutes of sun exposure could trigger another reaction. Over time, this fear can affect their daily routine, limiting social activities, outdoor exercise, and even simple errands.

articles.title: A little France in Pokhara
articles.summary:
The raclette arrives still bubbling.

At each table, diners slide slices of cheese beneath small raclette grills, watching them bubble and soften before pouring the melted cheese over boiled potatoes, vegetables and cured meat. Nearby, Hari Gurung stands behind the griddle preparing another order of buckwheat galettes, folding the savoury crêpes around mushrooms, eggs and locally made cheese.

Ten years ago, few people in Pokhara had heard of either dish. Today, they have become signature offerings at the French Crêperie.

It is an unlikely scene in a lakeside city better known for dal bhat, momo, and trekking cafés, but it reflects the idea that has shaped Gurung’s life: what he learned abroad could flourish at home.

As hundreds of thousands of Nepalis leave each year in search of opportunities abroad, Gurung chose to come back. After discovering Brittany’s food culture in western France, he returned convinced that many of the ingredients that define French country cooking were already growing in Nepal. His goal was never to recreate France, but to reinterpret its cuisine through a Nepali lens.

‘The recipes are French,” Gurung says. “The products are Nepali.”

At the French Crêperie in Pokhara, nearly every vegetable comes from nearby farms. Herbs are bought in local markets. Milk and cheese come from Nepali producers whenever possible. Only a handful of ingredients still arrive from overseas. The chalkboard menu shifts easily between French and English, offering naturally gluten-free galettes, croque-monsieurs, quiches and crêpes alongside local coffee, and Himalayan honey.

Before he was teaching Nepalis how to eat raclette or introducing trekkers to Breton galettes, he was a boy growing up in the hills of Gorkha near the Manaslu range. At the age of eight, he left his family in the hills of Gorkha to live with a family in Kathmandu who supported his education while he helped with household responsibilities.

Cooking was one of the few constants. He had been preparing meals for his family since he was eight years old, and what began as a household responsibility gradually became a profession. He started at the bottom, washing dishes in restaurant kitchens before discovering that he had a knack for cooking.

“I always wanted to do something for Nepal,” Gurung says. “Even when I was abroad, I thought about what I could bring back.”

That opportunity arrived unexpectedly through France, where during a visit he encountered a cuisine that felt both unfamiliar and surprisingly accessible. In Brittany, he became captivated by the region’s buckwheat galettes, savoury crêpes filled with eggs, cheese, vegetables, and cured meats. Beyond the recipes themselves, he admired the philosophy behind them. French country cooking relied on fresh produce, seasonal ingredients, and simple techniques rather than elaborate presentation.

As he travelled through France, Gurung began noticing something else. Many of the vegetables he saw in French markets already grew in Nepal.

“I would see produce there and think, ‘We have that in Nepal too,’” he says. “The spices are very similar. The flavour is just slightly different.”

The realisation was an epiphany for him, changing the way he thought about food. If the ingredients already existed at home, perhaps the recipes could too.

With the seeds of an idea, he returned to Nepal carrying far more than a cookbook.

Before opening the French Crêperie, Gurung experimented with another idea. In 2008, he opened a pizzeria. The business found customers quickly, but it also taught him something about Nepal’s restaurant industry.

“Everybody started opening pizzerias,” he says with a laugh. “There is a viral culture here. Once something becomes popular, everybody does the same thing.”

Gurung wanted his next venture to follow a different path. “I wanted to do something unique,” he says. “Something people couldn’t find anywhere else.”

The opportunity finally came in 2015, when he opened the French Crêperie near Phewa Lake.

The restaurant’s early years proved challenging. Specialty ingredients were difficult to source in Pokhara, forcing Gurung to make frequent trips to Kathmandu. Over time, as Nepal’s food industry evolved, many of those products became easier to find. Even today, he imports only the handful of ingredients that cannot be sourced domestically.

Choosing local ingredients is, for Gurung, an expression of confidence in Nepal — its farmers, its produce, and its potential. The restaurant reflects the same understanding that brought him home: that Nepal already has what it needs to build something meaningful.

When Gurung opened the French Crêperie, French food was still a novelty in Pokhara. Vegan and vegetarian restaurants were uncommon, and many locals had never heard of Breton galettes or raclette. Gurung wanted to build a restaurant where travellers and residents, meat eaters and vegetarians, could all find a place at the same table.

“I wanted to create a place where everyone could eat under one roof,” he says.

More than a decade later, the restaurant has become exactly that.

On any given afternoon, trekking guides stop in between tours, Nepali university students sample French cuisine for the first time, former migrant workers return in search of flavours they came to love in Europe, and families leave with sandwiches, lemon tarts, or Nutella crêpes before strolling along Phewa Lake.

One of those diners arrived in 2018 looking for a taste of home.

Colette, who grew up near Paris, was travelling through Nepal when she wandered into the French Crêperie. The menu caught her attention immediately.

So did the chef behind the griddle.

“It was love at first sight,” she says. “I came back a second time, then realised I wanted to come back to Nepal.” She eventually returned to Pokhara for good.

Today, Colette manages the restaurant’s Facebook and Instagram pages and works alongside Gurung and his wife and business partner. While Gurung prefers the kitchen, Colette enjoys telling the story behind it.

“Our love is like a recipe,” Gurung says. “We both contribute.”

As their relationship grew, so did Colette’s appreciation for the decision that had brought Gurung back to Nepal in the first place. “My husband could have lived abroad,” she says. “He chose to stay. To build here. To invest here. To create jobs here.”

“Opening a French restaurant in Nepal is a political gesture,” she says. “It is believing that you can help develop your country from within.”

Over the years, the restaurant has become a meeting place for travellers, expatriates and locals who gather over French recipes prepared with Nepali ingredients. Diplomats, aid workers and visitors regularly stop by, while the French ambassador has visited, drawn by a menu that feels familiar while celebrating local produce.

Most tables are filled with glasses of apple wine from Manang or homemade chyang rather than imported French wine, reflecting the restaurant's commitment to pairing French recipes with Nepali products wherever possible.

The French Crêperie has evolved into an informal meeting place where conversations flow as freely as the food. Travellers, expatriates and local residents gather around the same tables, swapping stories while French recipes prepared with Nepali ingredients provide common ground.

“We are more than a restaurant,” Colette says. “I love seeing French people meet Nepali people and for them to share their lives with each other.”

As another galette leaves the griddle and another bottle is uncorked, conversations drift between Nepali, French and English. For Gurung, that is the recipe he hoped to bring home — a reminder that Nepal already had the ingredients. It simply needed someone willing to see their potential.

articles.title: Documentary film review: The revolution that took their childhoods
articles.summary:
Robot Koenig’s ‘Returned: Child Soldiers of Nepal’s Maoist Army’ is a 2008 documentary film which follows the lives of a few of the many thousand child soldiers who have returned home after the end of the Nepali Civil War.

The documentary features the to-be-expected cast of journalists, scholars, experts, politicians and diplomats, but at its core are the child soldiers – their motivations in joining the war, their experience of the conflict and their difficult reintegration and return home.

The audience is first introduced to Ashish, who shares that he joined the war to fight for every Nepali’s right to food, clothing and shelter. As Ashish continues to share his story, however, it becomes evident his joining the ‘People’s Liberation Army’ was not entirely voluntary. The Maoist had come to Ashish’s village school to take them to a ‘cultural programme'. The students were to be returned home the next day.

Ashish’s narration of the exact events is unclear, but it would appear the Maoist leaders of the cultural programme had taken off with the children, including Ashish, who was 15 at the time.

Following the end of the war, Ashish returns home. He shares that he has wanted to continue his education, something he seems to have been unable to do, even after the war, owing to his family’s financial situation. Ashish’s father finds his son to have become more aloof. “He does not tell me anything. We don’t really talk," he says.

Some soldiers reflect back on their experiences proudly. Many from oppressed castes, soldiers enjoyed a certain power and dignity they were sure to be denied otherwise.

One young soldier, speaking anonymously, shares that he thought he kept his village peaceful during the conflict by shutting down card games, burning playing cards and silencing those he had felt disrespected by in the past. The soldier’s words feel misplaced. Here is a child maybe of 13 or 14, who ought to be in school reading poetry with his peers; in effect, it would appear, in charge of his village, dispensing justice as he sees fit.

Other soldiers seem to have joined the Maoists out of sheer childlike fascination. One young girl speaks of the Maoists with admiration. ‘These people live in the jungle. They can even take on the Royal Army with all their guns,” she says.

Preeti, who joined the People’s Liberation Army at 14, alleges then Royal Army raped women, looted houses, stole things and beat villagers. And that it was only after the village came under Maoist control that these activities stopped.

One child soldier, Ramesh, is motivated to join the guerrillas after the Royal Army took their father from their home, beat him and finally shot him to death at 4 a.m. one morning. His sister, however, stays back.

The documentary does a fine job showcasing the varying motivations and circumstances that led to the child soldiers joining the army.

No two stories are exactly the same, yet they share similar undercurrents. The lack of opportunities in the countryside, the inhumane realities of caste and gender, and the brutality brought on by the conflict, one finds, played a major role in convincing the children to pick up arms.

Similarly, no two returns are the same. And yet they too share similar undercurrents. The returned children are faced with a village and, on many occasions, a family which does not want them back. The children return from their fantastical lives as revolutionaries to a countryside which largely remains unchanged.

The women who fled their backward communities find themselves trying to reintegrate into those very same communities where they are now labelled ‘impure’ for having mingled with boys in the jungle.

One young girl shares the heartbreaking fate that was awaiting her upon her return. Upon her return, she is married off to an older man. She is only 14 at the time. When her new family finds out she used to be a Maoist soldier, they refuse to accept her. Beaten by her husband and abused by her in-laws, she tries, unsuccessfully, to hang herself.

Past the incessant use of Nepali folk music, Koenig’s film confronts viewers with uncomfortable questions, many of which have been lost in the public discourse in the two decades following the conflict.

Children, in the thousands, were plunged into a conflict they did not fully understand. And at the end of ten years, they found themselves just as poor, living in communities sometimes just as backwards and faced with additional discrimination and the reality of their lost childhoods.

The children in the documentary are largely uneducated and untrained in any income-generating trades.

In light of the Supreme Court’s recent decision on Lenin Bista’s writ, the film provides vivid images and stories of the conflict helpful in beginning to understand the 10 years of war, its ramifications, where we have come from, and where it remains for us to go.

Returned: Child Soldiers of Nepal's Maoist Army

Publisher: University of Cambridge

Direction, Production and Copyright: Robert Koenig

Duration: 60 minutes

Available on YouTube

articles.title: Fiction: Palpali dhakatopi pasal
articles.summary:
The hills of Tansen had always seemed eternal. From the stone-paved lanes of the old bazaar to the terraced fields that wrapped themselves around the slopes like green shawls, life moved slowly in the Palpa bazaar. The mornings smelled of wood smoke and fresh tea filled the air. Temple bells echoed through the surrounding hills. And in a small house overlooking the winding road, Mitralal and Saraswati had spent nearly five decades building a life together.

Their only son, Gokarna, owned a tiny shop named Palpali Dhakatopi Pasal in the main street of Tansen Bazaar.

The shop was not much to look at. Its wooden signboard had faded with age. Though the shop was small, it had a nice collection of all brands of Dhakatopis. The shop always filled Mitralal with pride and a sense of success. He neatly displayed traditional Dhakatopis on a wooden rack, displaying intricate patterns woven by skilled hands. Tourists bought them as souvenirs. Local men wore them during festivals and weddings. Government officials often stopped by to purchase one before important ceremonies.

To Gokarna, the shop was his grandfather's legacy. It was the thread that connected his family to generations of Nepali tradition. Every morning, Mitralal would worship the goddess Laxmi before meeting his customers.

But one winter, Mitralal's health began to fail rapidly. At first it was simple fatigue. Then came breathing difficulties. His legs weakened, and his memory sometimes wandered. Doctors in Tansen prescribed medicines and advised rest.

One cold morning, as mist rolled across the hills, Mitralal closed his eyes and never opened them again.

The funeral rites were performed beside the river. The smoke from the cremation pyre rose toward the pale sky. Saraswati stood silently. Her hands trembled. For fifty years she had shared every joy and hardship with her husband. Now the house felt unbearably empty. For many days at night she still reached toward his side of the bed before remembering he was gone.

Gokarna suffered too. He buried himself in work, opening the shop before sunrise and closing it long after dark.

Several months later, tragedy struck again. It happened on a stormy evening. A short circuit sparked inside the shop, and within minutes flames spread through the dry wooden shelves. By the time neighbours noticed, the fire had already engulfed the shop.

The bright Dhakatopis that had symbolised generations of labour burned like paper lanterns.

People formed lines carrying buckets of water. Someone called the fire brigade. But nothing could save the shop. When dawn arrived, only blackened beams remained. Gokarna stood in the ashes, staring silently.

The family had lost everything. Their only source of income was gone. For weeks Gokarna searched for solutions. He borrowed money from relatives and met lenders. But the money he had collected was not enough to rebuild their business once again. Finally, with tears in his eyes, he sat beside his mother.

"I have decided to go abroad."

Saraswati's heart sank. She looked at her son inquisitively.

“Ama, the money is not enough to begin the shop again. That’s why I want to go to Dubai”, said Gokarna.

"Dubai." Saraswati was surprised at her son’s decision.

"I found work in a garment factory. If I stay there for a few years, I can repay the loans and rebuild the shop once again." Saraswati looked at her son's face silently and nodded her head in affirmation.

"How long will you stay abroad?" she asked.

"Not long, Ama. As soon as I earn enough to rebuild our shop, I will return," said Gokarna and held his mother’s hands.

"I promise, Ama. One day we'll open a Dhakatopi shop that will be better than the previous one."

A few months later, he left. The bus carried him away through the winding roads. Saraswati stood atop a large boulder watching until the bus disappeared beyond the hills. Then she returned home alone.

The years that followed moved strangely. Days felt endless. Months disappeared quickly. Gokarna called whenever possible but sent money regularly.

Saraswati treasured every memory of her son. Yet loneliness slowly settled into the house like dust. Over the years, her eyesight began to deteriorate. At first she struggled to thread a needle.

Then faces became blurry. Eventually she could barely recognise visitors standing in front of her.

Doctors said her vision was failing badly. She had minor surgery on her eyes, but that too did not work. Her daily life activities became much more difficult. One evening, after a particularly difficult day, she spoke to Gokarna over the phone.

"My son, I don't know how much longer my eyes will last. At this moment, I don't need money anymore. I only want you to stay with me." Gokarna promised his mother to come home in a few days.

Then one midnight, as rain tapped softly against the roof, someone knocked on the door. Saraswati awoke immediately. Her heart raced.

"Who is it?"

"Ama." The voice was familiar. Her happiness knew no bounds.

"Yes." She hurried toward the door. The moment she touched his face, tears streamed down her cheeks.

"My son..."

Gokarna embraced his mother gently.

For the first time in years, the house felt alive again. That night they talked until dawn. Gokarna explained to his mother that he would be busy in the daytime arranging a new shop and meeting suppliers. He could not stay long during the day but return home at night. Saraswati did not mind. For her, the presence of her son was enough.

This became a daily routine for Gokarna. He would arrive home daily at midnight and bring delicious food with him. Both ate food together and talked and laughed late into the night.

For Saraswati, happiness returned. Neighbours, however, grew concerned. During the daytime she was almost always alone. No one saw Gokarna in the marketplace. No one saw him rebuilding a shop. Yet every time they asked, Saraswati smiled.

"During the daytime, my son is very busy at his shop, but he comes home daily at midnight”. At this, the neighbours exchanged worried glances but spoke nothing.

Then one afternoon, a government official arrived carrying a sealed envelope. He introduced himself politely and sat beside Saraswati.

"Ama, a body was found near Pokhara several months ago. It belonged to a young man. The face was badly damaged; that’s why the police could not identify him." The official hesitated but continued.

"We found documents suggesting he could be your son, Gokarna. So, the authority here in Palpa wants you to visit Pokhara for the DNA testing."

But Saraswati blasted in anger and asked the man to get out of her house immediately.

“My son is with me. At this very moment, he is at his shop. Don’t you know our shop? It is the Palpali Dhakatopi Pasal, one of the oldest shops in Palpa. Every evening, my son returns home, and we always have dinner together. Yet you claim that the police found my son’s body several months ago. How could that possibly be true when he is living with me? He spends his days busy at the shop, and every night he comes home with food. We sit down together and have dinner. So how can you say that my son died months ago?”

Looking at Saraswati, fuming with anger, the official man was scared and immediately left. However, the neighbours remained confused. After leaving for Dubai, the neighbours had never seen Gokarna in Tansen. The Palpali Dhakatopi Pasal was never rebuilt.

That night, some curious neighbours decided to wait until midnight to see Gokarna. They stood near the door patiently. It was midnight when Saraswati opened the door with a broad smile across her face and closed the door.

The neighbours hurried to the nearest window, eager to catch a glimpse of Gokarna. However, a thick curtain drawn across the window and the faint glow of a dim lamp prevented them from seeing clearly inside the room. Moments later, they heard the clinking of spoons against plates, followed by Saraswati's cheerful voice praising the delicious food. She continued talking for hours, as though engaged in a lively conversation, and now and then her laughter rang through the quiet night. The neighbours stood motionless, gripped by a mixture of fear and bewilderment. Unable to make sense of what they had witnessed, they slowly returned to their respective homes, their minds filled with confusion and unanswered questions.

Years have passed, but still people in Tansen Bazaar say that at midnight one can hear Saraswati talking with her son Gokarna.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.

articles.title: Nepali workers among injured in Qatar gas plant explosion, 13 killed
articles.summary:
Nepali workers were among those injured in an explosion and fire at a gas processing facility in Qatar, authorities said, as officials confirmed that 13 people were killed and 66 were injured in one of the country’s deadliest industrial accidents in recent years.

The blast occurred on Sunday night at the Barzan gas processing facility inside the Ras Laffan Industrial City complex, according to Qatar Energy officials. The injured include workers from Nepal, Qatar, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Kenya, Ghana, Tanzania and Nigeria. Authorities said none of the injured is in a critical condition.

Energy minister and president and CEO of QatarEnergy, Saad bin Sherida al-Kaabi, said in Doha that the incident was a “technical accident” and not linked to sabotage or hostile activity. He said emergency teams and civil defence units brought the fire under control quickly.

Al-Kaabi said production at the Barzan facility had been halted for maintenance since December 2025 and was restarted only two days before the incident. He added that Qatar’s liquefied natural gas operations, export systems and port facilities were not affected.

The people killed were Indian and Pakistani nationals, he said.

Al-Kaabi said Qatar has sufficient gas reserves and alternative supply capacity, and the country’s export commitments will not be affected. He also expressed condolences to the families of the deceased and wished the injured a speedy recovery.

Authorities have launched an investigation into the cause of the explosion, Reuters reported.

Al-Kaabi said the incident is under review, while reiterating that there is no impact on wider energy infrastructure.

Qatar hosts one of the world’s largest liquefied natural gas export hubs at Ras Laffan.

articles.title: हामीसँग हजार वर्षसम्म पुग्ने ग्यासोलिन भण्डार छ, चीनसँग छैन : राष्ट्रपति ट्रम्प
articles.summary:
अमेरिकी राष्ट्रपति डोनाल्ड ट्रम्पले अमेरिकासँग हजार वर्षसम्म पुग्ने ग्यासोलिन भण्डार रहेको दाबी गरेका छन्।

मिशिगनमा आयोजित एक चुनावी कार्यक्रममा उनले चीनलाई लक्षित गर्दै आफ्नो ऊर्जा र आर्थिक नीतिको बचाउ गरेका हुन्। राज्यको प्राइमरी चुनाव र आगामी मध्यावधि चुनाव नजिकिँदै गर्दा 'अमेरिका फर्स्ट' नीतिको जोडदार प्रचार गरिएको यो भाषणको मुख्य केन्द्रविन्दु चीन र अमेरिकी ऊर्जा बनेको थियो।

कार्यक्रमलाई सम्बोधन गर्दै ट्रम्पले चीनसँग कुनै पनि दीर्घकालीन ऊर्जा भण्डार नरहेको तर अमेरिकासँग हजार वर्षसम्म पुग्ने ग्यासोलिन भण्डार सुरक्षित रहेको दाबी गरेका हुन्। ‘हामीसँग हजार वर्षसम्म पुग्ने ग्यासोलिन भण्डार छ। चीनसँग छैन,’ उनले भने। ट्रम्पले अमेरिकासँग विशाल प्राकृतिक स्रोत रहेको भन्दै थप थपे, ‘हामीसँग बढी तेल छ। भेनेजुएला थप्दा त हामीसँग झन् धेरै तेल हुन्छ।’ यसमार्फत उनले अमेरिका र चीनबिचको आर्थिक तथा रणनीतिक प्रतिस्पर्धामा अमेरिका धेरै माथि रहेको स्पष्ट सन्देश दिन खोजेको पाइयो। यद्यपि, ऊर्जा विश्लेषकहरूका अनुसार ट्रम्पको 'हजार वर्षको भण्डार' सम्बन्धी दाबीलाई आधिकारिक वैज्ञानिक अनुमान भन्दा पनि राजनीतिक रणनीतिका रूपमा हेरिएको छ।

यो भाषण आगामी मध्यावधि चुनावलाई लक्षित गर्दै दिइएको हो। हाल इरान युद्धका कारण अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजारमा तेलको मूल्य बढेर आपूर्तिमा चुनौती देखिएको छ। इरान युद्धले होर्मुज जलमार्गबाट हुने तेल निर्यातमा अवरोध पुग्दा अमेरिकामा पनि पेट्रोलको मूल्य प्रभावित भएको छ। बाँकी विश्वजस्तै अमेरिकी अर्थतन्त्र पनि दबाबमा परेको छ। यसै सन्दर्भमा ट्रम्पले अमेरिकी ऊर्जा स्वतन्त्रता र दीर्घकालीन भण्डारलाई मुख्य राजनीतिक हतियार बनाएका हुन्।

चीनसँगको रणनीतिक प्रतिस्पर्धाको कुरा गर्दै ट्रम्पले विगतका नेताहरूले अमेरिकी रोजगारी विदेश पठाएको तर आफ्नो प्रशासनले अमेरिकी कामदारहरूलाई सधैँ पहिलो प्राथमिकता दिएको बताए। उनले भने, ‘मिशिगनका अटो कामदारहरूका लागि अन्ततः एउटा राष्ट्रपति आएको छ, जसले मिशिगन र अमेरिकालाई पहिलो प्राथमिकता दिन्छ।’

उनले थप भने, ‘मैले तपाईंहरूका लागि तपाईंका आमाबाबुले भन्दा बढी गरेको छु।’ सो अवसरमा उनले अमेरिकामा अटो कारखाना र प्लान्टहरू इतिहासकै उच्च गतिमा निर्माण भइरहेको समेत दाबी गरेका थिए।

भाषणकै क्रममा राष्ट्रपति ट्रम्प डेमोक्रेटिक पार्टीभित्रका प्रगतिशील नेताहरूमाथि समेत आक्रामक देखिए। चुनावी र्‍यालीमा भएका केही प्रदर्शनकारीहरूलाई लक्षित गर्दै उनीहरूलाई 'कम्युनिस्ट' को संज्ञा दिएर चेतावनी दिँदै भने, ‘मैले कहिल्यै यो समाजवादी देश बन्दैन भनेको थिएँ, तर अब उनीहरू यसलाई कम्युनिस्ट बनाउन चाहन्छन्। यो देशको लागि इतिहासकै ठूलो खतरा हो।’ उनले यस्ता नीतिहरूले देशलाई कंगाल बनाउने, जनतालाई गरिबी र डरमा बाँच्न बाध्य पार्ने तथा देशमा प्रहरी र दमकलसमेत नहुने अवस्था आउने गम्भीर आरोप लगाए।

articles.title: सर्वसाधारणलाई कहिले खुल्छ सुरुङ ?
articles.summary:
नागढुंगा–सिस्ने खोला सुरुङमार्ग सोमबारबाट सञ्चालनमा आएको छ। निर्माण थालेको ८० महिनापछि सुरुङमार्ग सञ्चालनमा आएको हो। पहिलो चरणमा एम्बुलेन्स, दमकल र सुरक्षाकर्मीको गाडीका लागि चौबिसै घण्टा सुरुङ खुला हुने छ। सुरुङ सञ्चालनका लागि आवश्यक जनशक्ति तयार नहुँदा आम सर्वसाधारणले त्यसको प्रयोग कहिलेदेखि गर्न पाउने भन्ने अझै निश्चित भएको छैन।

पहिलो चरणमा तीन महिनालाई परीक्षणकाल भनिए पनि सुरुङ सञ्चालनका लागि आवश्यक जनशक्तिको व्यवस्थापन हुन नसक्दा सर्वधारणका लागि भने अझै सुरुङयात्रा निश्चित छैन। आवश्यक तयारी र जनशक्तिको व्यवस्थापनभन्दा उद्घाटनमा हतारो गर्ने विगतलाई निरन्तरता दिँदै वर्तमान सरकारले पनि सुरुङ उद्घाटन गरेको हो। ४२ महिनाभित्र काम सक्ने लक्ष्यसहित तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री केपी शर्मा ओलीले चन्द्रागिरी नगरपालिका–२ स्थित टुटीपाखामा २०७६ कात्तिक ४ गते सुरुङको शिलान्यास गरेका थिए। आयोजनामा १६ अर्ब रुपैयाँ जाइकाको सहुलियतपूर्ण ऋण छ भने मुआब्जालगायत कुल निर्माण खर्च २४ अर्ब खर्च रहेको आयोजनाले जनाएको छ।

खर्च जोगिन्छ कि बढ्छ ?

सुरुङमार्गको उद्घाटनसँगै नेपालको सडक मार्ग नयाँ चरणमा प्रवेश गरेको छ। तर यति ठुलो रकम खर्चेर निर्माण गरिएको सुरुङ मार्गबाट आम सर्वधारणका लागि लागत र लगानी जोगियो या अझ खर्च बढ्यो भन्ने प्रश्न जन्मिएको छ। दुई र तीन पांग्रे सवारीका साथै प्रज्वलनशील पदार्थ बोकेका सवारीसाधनले सुरुङ मार्ग प्रयोग गर्न पाउने छैनन्। जसले सुरुङमार्ग प्रयोग गर्न पाउने छन्, उनीहरूले त्यसबापत ६० रुपैयाँ देखि ६०० रुपैयाँसम्म शुल्क तिनुपर्ने हुन्छ। यो सुरुङले पुरानो राजमार्गभन्दा केवल २.६८ किलोमिटर मात्र दुरी घट्ने छ। सुरुङमार्गको दुरी २.६८ किलोमिटर छ। त्यसबाहेक पहुँच सडकमा पुग्न पूर्वतर्फ २.३२० र पश्चिम ०.५६५ किलोमिटर दुरी छ।

निर्माण थालेको ८० महिनापछि परीक्षण सञ्चालनमा आएको नागढुंगा–सिस्ने खोला सुरुङमार्गको प्रयोग सर्वसाधारणले कहिलेदेखि गर्न पाउने भन्ने अझै निश्चित छैन।

यात्राका लागि ठुला सवारीसाधनले ६०० रुपैयाँसम्म शुल्क बुझाउँदा यसबाट यात्रा झनै महँगो पर्ने देखिएको छ। यद्यपि सडक विभागका महानिर्देशक डा. विजय जैशीले सुरुङमार्ग प्रयोग गर्ने सवारीसाधनको समय र पैसा दुवै बचत हुने बताए। ‘उकालोमा तेल बढी खान्छ, एक नम्बर गियरमा उकालो चढाउनुपर्छ। उकालोमा गाडी गुडाउँदा इन्जिनको चाप बढ्छ तर सुरुङमार्ग प्रयोग गर्दा इन्जिनको चाप घट्छ,’ महानिर्देशक जैशीले भने, ‘सुरुङमार्ग प्रयोग नगरी सवारीसाधनलाई उक्त सडकमा यात्रा पूरा गर्न ३० मिनेट लाग्छ तर प्रयोग गर्दा सात मिनेटमै यात्रा पूरा हुन्छ। यसबाट २३ मिनेट समय बच्छ। लामो समयसम्म ट्राफिक जाममा पर्ने झन्झट बेहोर्नुपर्दैन।’ उनका अनुसार सुरुङमार्ग प्रयोग गर्दा सबैभन्दा ठुलो फाइदा ट्राफिक सुरक्षा हो। ‘सुरुङमार्ग प्रयोग नगर्दा दुर्घटनाको सम्भावना रहिरन्छ तर प्रयोग गर्दा दुर्घटनाको सम्भावना करिबकरिब हुँदैन।’ विभागका अनुसार सिस्नेखोला–बलम्बु जोड्ने सुरुङमार्गबाट २.८ किलोमिटर दुरी घट्ने भएको छ।

शुल्क कति छ ?

सुरुङमार्ग प्रयोग गरेबापत काठमाडौं प्रवेश गर्ने र काठमाडौंबाट धादिङ प्रवेश गर्ने सवारीसाधनका हकमा फरकफरक शुल्क राखिएको छ। कार, भ्यान, पिकअप, ट्याक्टर, माइक्रो बस र अन्य हलुका सवारीसाधन काठमाडौं प्रवेश गर्दा ६५ रूपैयाँ र बाहिरिँदा ६० रुपैयाँ शुल्क बुझाउनुपर्ने छ। यसैगरी मिनी बस, मिनी टिपर/ट्रकको प्रवेशका लागि ११५ रुपैयाँ, बाहिरिँदा ८० रुपैयाँ तथा बस, ट्रक (सिंगल रियर एक्सल) लाई प्रवेश गर्दा २६० रुपैयाँ र बाहिरिँदा २०० रुपैयाँ शुल्क बुझाउनुपर्छ। यसैगरी मल्टी एक्सल ट्रक/सवारीसाधन तथा भारी उपकरणका हकमा प्रवेश गर्नुपरे ६०० रुपैयाँ र बाहिरिँदा २५० रुपैयाँ शुल्क बुझाउनुपर्ने हुन्छ। जुन अहिलेको पेट्रोलियम पदार्थको मूल्यलाई नै आधार बनाउने हो भने हलुका सवारीसाधनभन्दा मालवाहक सवारीसाधनको खर्च थप बढ्ने छ।

तत्काल कुनकुन सवारी गुड्छन् ?

अहिले सबै किसिमका सवारीसाधनले सुरुङमार्ग प्रवेश गर्न पाउँदैनन्। हाल दमकल, एम्बुलेन्स, सुरक्षाकर्मीका सवारीसाधनलगायत सवारीले मात्र सुरुङमार्ग प्रवेश गर्ने छन्। विभागका अनुसार केही समय परीक्षण सञ्चालन अवधि रहने छ। उक्त अवधिमा अन्य सवारीसाधनलाई समेत क्रमशः चरणबद्ध रूपमा प्रवेश गराई सुरुङको सुरक्षा प्रणाली, सञ्चालन व्यवस्था तथा आपतकालीन प्रतिकार्य प्रणालीको परीक्षण गरिने छ।

परीक्षण सञ्चालन अवधिभर सुरुङ प्रयोगबापत कुनै टोल दस्तुर लिइने छैन। परीक्षण सञ्चालन सफलतापूर्वक सम्पन्न भई सुरुङमार्ग नियमित रूपमा सञ्चालनमा आएपछि तोकिएको दरअनुसार टोल दस्तुर संकलन गरिने छ। विभागका अनुसार टोल व्यवस्थापनलाई आधुनिक र प्रभावकारी बनाउन आरएफआइडीमा आधारित विद्युतीय टोल संकलन प्रणाली जडान गरिएको छ। सडक बोर्ड नेपालबाट स्वीकृत आरएफआइडी पास तोकिएका बैंकमार्फत उपलब्ध छन् भने अन्य अधिकृत बैंकहरूले पनि उक्त प्रणालीमा आबद्ध हुने कार्य अन्तिम चरणमा रहेको विभागको भनाइ छ।

विभागका अनुसार मुख्य सुरुङ २.६८८ किलोमिटर लामो छ। उक्त सुरुङमार्ग दुई लेनमा सञ्चालन हुने छ। यसको चौडाइ ११ मिटर तथा उचाइ ८.१५ मिटरको छ। यसैगरी आपतकालीन सुरुङ २.५५७ किलोमिटर लामो छ। यसको चौडाइ ५.१ मिटर छ भने उचाइ चार मिटर छ। यसैगरी मुख्य सुरुङ र आपतकालीन सुरुङबिच करिब प्रत्येक ३७५ मिटरमा सात वटा क्रस प्यासेज पहुँच मार्ग राखिएका छन्। यस आयोजनामा पुल, कल्भर्ट, फ्लाइओभर तथा अन्य १२ वटा संरचना तयार गरिएका छन्। हाल सुरुङमार्गसँग जोडिएको राजमार्ग भएर दैनिक करिब १३ हजार सवारीसधान आवतजात गर्ने जनाइएको छ।

articles.title: काँकरभिट्टाबाट गत आवमा साढे नौ हजार विदेशी पर्यटक भित्रिए
articles.summary:
नेपालको पूर्वी नाका काँकरभिट्टा स्थलमार्ग हुँदै गत आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ मा नौ हजार चार सय ४७ जना विदेशी पर्यटक नेपाल भित्रिएका छन्।

अध्यागमन कार्यालय काँकरभिट्टाका निमित्त प्रमुख इन्द्रकुमार राजवंशीका अनुसार उक्त अवधिमा दैनिक सरदर २६ जना विदेशी पर्यटक यो नाका भएर नेपाल प्रवेश गरेका हुन्। छिमेकी मुलुक भारतका नागरिकका लागि भिसा अनिवार्य नभएकाले यो तथ्याङ्कमा भारतीय पर्यटकको सङ्ख्या समावेश गरिएको छैन।

नाकाबाट कूल ८६ देशका नागरिक आवतजावत गरे पनि सबैभन्दा बढी भुटानी पर्यटक भित्रिएका छन्। कूल आगमनको ५३ प्रतिशतअर्थात् चार हजार नौ सय ९४ जना भुटानी नागरिक रहेका छन्। यस्तै, दोस्रो स्थानमा अमेरिकाका नागरिक रहेका छन्, जहाँबाट २३ प्रतिशतअर्थात् दुई हजार एक सय ५२ जना पर्यटक भित्रिएका निमित्त प्रमुख राजवंशीले जानकारी दिए।

कार्यालयको तथ्याङ्कअनुसार पूर्वी नाकामा पुस र माघ महिनालाई मुख्य पर्यटकीय यामको रूपमा लिइएको छ। सबैभन्दा बढी पुस महिनामा एक हजार आठ सय ५० जना पर्यटक नेपाल भित्रिएका थिए भने सबैभन्दा कम भदौ महिनामा दुई सय १६ जना मात्र आएका थिए।

पुस र माघ महिनामा भुटानमा जाडो बिदा हुने भएकाले त्यहाँका नागरिक झापा तथा वरपर रहेका आफन्त भेटघाट गर्न र पूर्वको पशुपतिनाथका रूपमा परिचित खोटाङको हलेसी महादेवको दर्शन एवं तीर्थयात्राका लागि आउने गरेकाले सो समयमा चाप बढेको निमित्त प्रमुख राजवंशीको भनाइ छ।

अध्यागमन कार्यालयले सन् २०२४ अगस्टदेखि मात्र यस नाकाबाट पूर्ण रूपमा अध्यागमन सेवा सुरु गरेकाले धेरै विदेशी पर्यटकलाई यो नाका प्रयोग गर्नेबारे अझै पर्याप्त जानकारी भइनसकेको कार्यालयले जनाएको छ। रासस

articles.title: यस्तो छ आजका लागि कृषिउपजको थोक मूल्य
articles.summary:
